newsitem.title: USA: U.S. corn donation hailed but self-help vital.
newsitem.headline: U.S. corn donation hailed but self-help vital.

text.p: The U.S. decision to donate an additional 50,000 metric tons of corn to North Korea was hailed Tuesday by analysts and aid officials who saw barters as a possible way for North Korea to acquire food on its own.

Representative Tony Hall, who saw widespread hunger during a recent visit to North Korea, said the $15 million U.S. donation was "not enough" but "a very good first step" that would encourage other nations to provide assistance.
"We saw a lot of people in the fields, picking weeds and grass for nutrition, to put in their soup," said Hall, Ohio Democrat, who recounted talking to people who had not eaten in a day.

Douglas Coutts, head of the North American office of the U.N. World Food Program, said the U.S. donation was "very good news." The agency has requested nations to donate 200,000 metric tons of food to avert famine in North Korea.

Senator Pat Roberts, Kansas Republican, said the new donation was consistent with congressional desire for hunger relief while not yielding on the need for North Korea "must sit down at the table" for negotiations for peace on the Korean peninsula.

Speaking to the Korea Society of Washington, Coutts said a zinc-for-wheat barter announced earlier this month between Pyongyang and Cargill Inc, the huge U.S. grains merchant, showed the potential for North Korea to met its food needs in the longer term through commercial channels rather than rely on aid. "We
are hoping commercial concerns in the (commodity) trade might consider this an opportunity to get involved in North Korea," Coutts said.
The barter with Cargill reportedly involved 20,000 tons of white wheat for 4,000 tons of zinc. Cargill held a U.S. license allowing up to 500,000 tons of wheat and rice sales.

Another analyst, John Dyck of the Economic Research Service at the U.S. Agriculture Department, said it would take several years for North Korea to become a fully commercial market. He said he would expect to see more small-scale purchases, similar to the barter with Cargill.

Victor Cha, a Georgetown University professor who specializes in East Asian matters, and Dyck noted North Korea owed huge debts on past trading. Dyck said North Korea would have to improve its standing if it was to become a regular cash customer for U.S. grains.
North Korea probably would look for wheat, rice and corn imports with corn dominating because of lower prices, he said.
Cha said barter rarely has been an effective tool in trade with North Korea. Cargill, he said, appeared to be "getting its foot in the door" with hopes of larger sales in the future.

The professor said there "has been a form of tacit reciprocity" although all sides have denied linkage between food aid and efforts to arrange four-nation peace talks. It suggested North Korea "will come back in a positive nature" on proposal for four-nation negotiations. Private consultant John Schnittker
said the corn donation was a wise step by the Clinton administration. It would help avoid starvation in North Korea, he said, and "we won't miss it either" because of adequate U.S. grain stockpiles.

Meanwhile, the charity World Vision announced a total of 75 tons of vegetable seeds would leave U.S. ports on Wednesday and Friday, bound for North Korea. The shipment included broccoli, cucumber, carrot, lettuce, onion, pepper, tomato, green bean and pea seeds donated by Asgrow Seeds.
